title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
contentHtml:
I don’t mean to suggest that FiveThirtyEight invented the concept of systematic polling error, but the FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin forecasts have accounted for it since their inception. It’s why we gave Trump a ~30 percent chance of winning the 2016 election when some of our competitors literally put the odds at 1 percent. Our model assumed that if Hillary Clinton lost Michigan, for instance, she’d probably lose Pennsylvania too.

The models that wrongly treated races as a series of independent coin flips have died out, and deservedly so. But I’m just gonna be honest … I wish there were still a couple of models like that that could serve as a foil to FLIPR. It would be nice to position the Silver Bulletin forecast as being in the sensible middle ground. I can’t say something like “sure, Democrats are favorites, but Model XYZ has them at 92 percent to win the Senate? That’s crazy!” Nobody, whether they have a model or not, seems to think that. Everyone still remembers 2016 — and 2020 and 2024.

But just for fun, what would a coin-flip type model say this year? Well, Democrats currently lead in the polls in enough states to claim a 54-46 Senate majority. Many of those leads are modest, and in some cases, the “fundamentals” that FLIPR considers push things back toward 50/50. Still, if you treated each race as independent and ran a simple Monte Carlo simulation based on our “Deluxe” win probabilities in each race, you’d get a 91 percent chance of Democrats winning the Senate.

FLIPR’s actual Senate odds for Democrats have improved substantially since Labor Day, but because we account for both national and regional correlated errors, we’re not particularly close to that, with a mid-70s win probability instead. This is much closer to assuming races are perfectly correlated than perfectly independent.1

To be fair, we are a little bit on the higher side of the consensus for Democrats this year. There are reasonable differences of opinion on how to model these errors, how to blend polls and fundamentals, how aggressively to update one’s averages, and so forth. I don’t necessarily know every assumption that goes into every model. But there aren’t the sort of “Model Wars” that we used to see. Most of our competitors’ forecasts look basically reasonable to me.

Broken polls are like a recipe that misses the mark — not a broken gauge

So what’s the “pet peeve” that I teased in the headline? When you see someone like Frank Luntz go on TV and talk about how polls may be undersampling Republicans, he seems to be operating under an assumption that the entire election analysis community went on a long hiking expedition after the 2014 midterm and hasn’t looked at an election result since. We’d be in for quite a few surprises. Donald Trump was elected president twice, pulling off a Grover Cleveland even after he’d been impeached for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 election? Georgia is now a swing state … but Florida isn’t? The New York Fucking Knicks won the NBA title?

If nobody had changed anything since 2016, my expectation is that you’d be seeing some unrealistically rosy numbers for Democrats. Luntz isn’t wrong that certain Republican-leaning voters are less likely to respond to polls. GOP voters have lower social trust. They’re also less likely to have college degrees, and “noncollege” voters are considerably less likely to respond to surveys.

However, pollsters are acutely aware of this problem. How couldn’t they be? That doesn’t mean they’ve solved it, because willingness to answer a poll is correlated with voting Democratic, and that’s inherently tricky. But pollsters have a variety of tactics and techniques to combat it. They can match to Census Bureau demographics, or they can anchor to the past reported vote. Or there might be approaches that are a little bit more subjective: for instance, playing around with assumptions in likely voter models. Pollsters might herd or refuse to publish results they deem too far out of consensus; it’s happened before in the U.S. and abroad.

The death knell for pollsters who stuck to old gold-standard techniques, even when it produced apparent outliers, was the Ann Selzer poll the weekend before the 2024 election that incorrectly showed Kamala Harris winning the Hawkeye State. Selzer not only left election polling;2 Donald Trump sued her. (Trump’s lawsuit was eventually dismissed.) I’ve always thought Selzer’s decision to publish the Harris +3 was gutsy — but it was gutsy precisely because there would be big consequences if her poll was wrong.
